metadata.title: Examining ICT attitudes, use and support in blended learning settings for students’ reading performance: Approaches of artificial intelligence and multilevel model

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for reading literacy and merges it with World Bank GDP per capita, then restricts the analytic sample to students in blended test language classes who completed the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. For the multilevel (HLM) stage, the authors explicitly state that student weights were implemented to account for the design effects in the PISA data, indicating complex survey weighting was applied in the inferential multilevel models. The RF stage is described as a regression RF with 10-fold cross-validation; the manuscript does not specify weight-aware RF training, so weighting is primarily documented for the HLM stage. The data cleaning includes deletion of repeated values and outliers and multiple imputation for missing questionnaire variables, which is applied before model fitting; thus, the weighted HLM estimates reflect both the PISA design and the imputed covariates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: From PISA 2018, students from 32 OECD countries who completed the optional ICT familiarity questionnaires were selected. The analytic sample further uses students’ reading scores (PISA 2018 reading literacy) for those in blended test language classes, classified using questionnaire item IC152Q01HA into four ICT-use classroom types; students selecting categories where teachers alone used ICT, students alone used ICT, or both used ICT were included (categories 1, 2, and 3). The analysis controls for demographic and school factors and includes only the specified ICT-related constructs derived from student, school, and ICT familiarity questionnaires; missing covariates were handled via multiple imputation (m=10) and outliers/repeated values were removed during cleaning.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teacher ICT use support from school

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds, blended test language classes; 32 OECD countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (10-fold cross-validation): MSE=6319.33, MAE=63.19, R²=0.38; optimal feature set retained 27 factors; feature importance ranked ESCS (1st), USESCH (2nd), INTICT (3rd), HOMESCH (4th), ENTUSE (5th).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy data from blended test language classes across 32 OECD countries, the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), ICT use at school (USESCH), interest in ICT (INTICT), ICT use outside for schoolwork (HOMESCH), and ICT use outside for entertainment (ENTUSE) to predict students’ reading performance (plausible values), finding that the optimal ICT-related feature set (27 factors) achieved R²=0.38 with ESCS and school ICT use ranking highest in relative importance. This indicates that blended reading outcomes are most strongly associated with students’ background and the intensity of ICT use in school, suggesting that policy should prioritize structured, school-based ICT integration rather than assuming that ICT access alone will improve reading.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 reading literacy for 15-year-olds in blended test language classes, selecting students from 32 OECD countries who completed the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire (total N=152,218; 9,087 schools). The authors combine a Random Forest regression (10-fold cross-validation) with a three-level hierarchical linear model (HLM) using PISA’s 10 plausible values and multiple imputation for missing covariates (m=10). In the RF stage, the optimal ICT-related feature set retained 27 factors and produced MSE=6319.33, MAE=63.19, and R²=0.38; feature importance ranked ESCS first and ICT use at school (USESCH) second, followed by interest in ICT (INTICT), ICT use outside for schoolwork (HOMESCH), and ICT use outside for entertainment (ENTUSE). In the multilevel stage, student and school ICT factors show both linear and curvilinear (quadratic) associations, and school ICT quality moderates several student-level relationships. Limitations include cross-sectional inference (no causal identification) and the fact that RF is not described as weight-aware, while HLM explicitly applies PISA student weights.
